subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statement best defines osmosis?
options: The movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
The active movement of mineral ions into a cell using energy
The movement of any molecule from high to low concentration
The evaporation of water from the surface of a leaf
questions.explain: Osmosis is the net movement of water from a region of higher water concentration (dilute) to lower water concentration (concentrated) across a partially permeable membrane.

questions.q: Osmosis takes place across which type of membrane?
questions.explain: A partially permeable membrane lets small water molecules pass but blocks larger solute molecules.

questions.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to the cell?
options: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid
Water leaves by osmosis and the cell becomes flaccid
Water leaves and the cell membrane pulls away from the wall
No net movement of water occurs
questions.explain: Pure water is more dilute than the cell contents, so water enters by osmosis and the cell swells and becomes turgid.

questions.q: What term describes a plant cell that is firm and full of water?
questions.explain: A turgid cell is swollen and firm because water has entered by osmosis, pushing the membrane against the cell wall.

questions.q: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated sugar solution. Which change occurs?
options: Water leaves the cell and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis)
Water enters and the cell bursts
Mineral ions leave the cell by osmosis
questions.explain: The external solution is more concentrated, so water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell becomes plasmolysed.

questions.q: Potato chips of equal mass are left in different solutions. A chip in strong salt solution is reweighed. What is the most likely result?
questions.explain: The salt solution is more concentrated than the cell contents, so water leaves the cells by osmosis and mass decreases.

questions.q: What does the xylem transport in a plant?
questions.explain: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots upward to the leaves.

questions.q: What does the phloem mainly transport?
questions.explain: Phloem carries dissolved food (mainly sucrose) from the leaves to other parts of the plant.

questions.q: A plant tissue is made of dead, hollow tubes with no end walls, strengthened by lignin. Which tissue is it and what does it carry?
questions.explain: Dead, hollow, lignified tubes describe xylem, which transports water and mineral ions.

questions.q: What is the name of the transport of dissolved sugars in the phloem?
questions.explain: Translocation is the movement of dissolved sugars through the phloem.

questions.q: How does a root hair cell increase the uptake of water from the soil?
options: It has a long extension giving a large surface area for osmosis
It contains chloroplasts to make water
It has a thick waxy cuticle
questions.explain: The root hair increases surface area, speeding up water absorption by osmosis.

questions.q: Unlike xylem, in which direction can substances move in the phloem?
options: In both directions, up and down the plant
Only upwards from roots to leaves
Only downwards from leaves to roots
questions.explain: Phloem is made of living cells and can transport sugars in both directions, whereas xylem carries water only upwards.

questions.q: A stem is placed in dye and the coloured tubes are found stained after an hour. Which tissue has carried the dye and water?
questions.explain: Xylem transports water (and the dissolved dye) up the stem, so these vessels become stained.

questions.q: What is transpiration?
options: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant
The uptake of minerals by the roots
The transport of sugars in the phloem
The production of glucose in photosynthesis
questions.explain: Transpiration is the evaporation and diffusion of water vapour from the leaves, mainly through the stomata.

questions.q: Through which structures is most water vapour lost from a leaf?
questions.explain: Stomata are pores, mainly on the underside of the leaf, through which water vapour escapes.

questions.q: How does increasing the temperature affect the rate of transpiration?
questions.explain: Higher temperature increases evaporation of water from the leaf cells, raising the transpiration rate.

questions.q: How does increasing humidity of the surrounding air affect transpiration?
options: It increases water uptake by roots
questions.explain: High humidity reduces the concentration gradient of water vapour between leaf and air, slowing transpiration.

questions.q: Why does moving air (wind) increase the rate of transpiration?
options: It removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the gradient steep
It adds water vapour to the leaf surface
It cools the leaf and stops evaporation
questions.explain: Wind blows away accumulated water vapour, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient so more water escapes.

questions.q: In which set of conditions would a plant transpire fastest?
questions.explain: High temperature, low humidity and air movement all increase transpiration, so together they give the fastest rate.

questions.q: Which cells open and close the stomata?
questions.explain: Pairs of guard cells surround each stoma and change shape to open or close the pore.
